pathophysiology.summary: Initial clinical assessment must differentiate small bowel obstruction (SBO) from large bowel obstruction (LBO). Mechanical obstruction causes proximal dilatation, gas and fluid accumulation, third-space loss, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and acute kidney injury; rising pressure or a closed loop can cause strangulation, ischaemia, perforation and peritonitis.
keyMechanisms: SBO is commonly caused by adhesions from prior surgery; other causes include incarcerated hernia, Crohn disease, intussusception and volvulus.
LBO is commonly caused by colorectal carcinoma; other causes include sigmoid or caecal volvulus, diverticular strictures and faecal impaction.
A competent ileocaecal valve can create a closed loop in LBO, with rapid caecal distension and increased perforation risk as diameter rises.
Rising intraluminal pressure or closed-loop twisting compromises venous then arterial flow, causing strangulation, ischaemia, perforation and peritonitis.
Physical examination may miss strangulation, so CT and laboratory markers are important in risk assessment.

symptoms: SBO: rapid-onset severe colicky periumbilical pain, early frequent bilious vomiting, and progressive distension.
LBO: gradual dull hypogastric or lower-abdominal pain, prominent generalised distension, and late or absent vomiting.
Absolute constipation or no flatus may occur late in SBO and early in LBO.
physicalSigns: Assess for peritonitis: involuntary guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness and constant severe pain.
Assess for ischaemia or strangulation: fever, persistent tachycardia, shock and raised lactate.
Examine all hernial orifices for an incarcerated or irreducible hernia.
Review CT for closed-loop obstruction, reduced wall enhancement, pneumoperitoneum or marked caecal dilatation.
redFlags: Peritonitis or constant severe pain — escalate to surgery immediately.
Fever, persistent tachycardia, refractory shock or lactate above 2.0 mmol/L suggesting ischaemia or strangulation.
CT showing closed-loop obstruction, reduced bowel-wall enhancement, free air or caecal diameter above 12 cm.
Irreducible groin or abdominal-wall hernia with skin change or severe tenderness.
precipitants: Previous abdominal surgery, hernia, Crohn disease, tumour, volvulus, diverticular stricture or faecal impaction.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Absent bowel sounds, diffuse dilatation without a transition point on CT, often postoperative or electrolyte-driven; treat the underlying cause.
Massive colonic dilatation without a mechanical block on CT; management may include neostigmine or endoscopic decompression.
Severe pain out of proportion to examination, high lactate and arterial or venous thrombus on CT angiography; requires emergency vascular or bowel surgery.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 10.0 × 10⁹/L or leukopenia may occur; interpret with the clinical picture.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Leukocytosis or leukopenia may support inflammation or ischaemia and should prompt surgical review when combined with concerning findings.

clinicalManagement.title: SBO: resuscitation and initial measures
actions: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloids and correct electrolyte deficits, prioritising potassium replacement.
Insert a wide-bore 16–18 Fr nasogastric tube to low continuous suction when indicated.
Give intravenous analgesia and antiemetics and keep the patient strictly nil by mouth.

clinicalManagement.title: SBO: diagnostic imaging and triage
actions: Perform urgent CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.
If CT confirms uncomplicated ASBO without ischaemia, free fluid or closed loop, proceed to a monitored non-operative trial.

clinicalManagement.title: SBO: non-operative trial and contrast protocol
actions: For uncomplicated ASBO, administer 50–100 mL water-soluble contrast via the nasogastric tube and clamp for 1–2 hours according to local protocol.
Obtain a follow-up abdominal X-ray at 24 hours.

Contrast in the colon supports continued conservative management; absent contrast at 24 hours, clinical deterioration or persistent high tube output after 72 hours indicates failure and need for surgery.

branches.condition: Peritonitis, ischaemia, closed loop or clinical deterioration
actions: Do not prolong non-operative management; escalate urgently to surgery.

clinicalManagement.title: SBO: operative intervention
actions: Operate for peritonitis or ischaemia on initial assessment, or failure of the 72-hour non-operative trial.
Use open laparotomy or carefully selected laparoscopic adhesiolysis; consider adhesion barriers according to the operative plan.

clinicalManagement.title: LBO: emergency stabilisation and triage
actions: Resuscitate with balanced crystalloids, monitor continuously and keep the patient nil by mouth.
Do not apply the Gastrografin challenge designed for uncomplicated SBO.

clinicalManagement.title: LBO: aetiology-specific management
actions: Malignant obstruction: prepare for urgent resection or a self-expanding metallic stent as a bridge to elective surgery according to specialist assessment.
Sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic decompression and rectal tube when there is no gangrene or perforation; plan definitive surgery during the same admission.
Caecal volvulus: endoscopic decompression is rarely effective; arrange operative management such as ileocaecal resection or right hemicolectomy.

branches.condition: Gangrene or perforation in sigmoid volvulus
actions: Skip endoscopic decompression and proceed to emergency laparotomy with the appropriate resection and stoma strategy.

medicationPlan.note: The WSES Bologna guideline does not specify drug or contrast doses. Use local protocols for analgesia, antiemetics, fluids, electrolytes and water-soluble contrast volume.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Peritonitis, strangulation or bowel ischaemia (clinical, lactate, or CT: closed loop, ischaemia, free fluid)
ASBO without the above — up to 72 h
In colon = likely resolution; not in colon = likely failure

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute bowel obstruction in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Relying on examination to exclude strangulation (sensitivity about 48%).
Prolonging non-operative treatment beyond 72 h without progress.
keyPoints: CT with water-soluble contrast is the key test.
Otherwise NG decompression, fluids and electrolytes for up to 72 h.
Contrast in the colon at 24 h predicts success.

patientEducation: Explain recurrence warning signs: cramping pain, persistent vomiting and increasing abdominal swelling.
Seek urgent care if symptoms recur or oral intake is not tolerated.
lifestyleAndDiet: Resume oral intake only after clinical improvement and according to the surgical plan.
Arrange dietitian review after prolonged nil-by-mouth status when clinically indicated.
mdtReferrals: General Surgery review for suspected obstruction and all red flags.
Dietitian review when prolonged nil-by-mouth status or nutritional risk is present.
dischargeCriteria: Obstruction resolved with passage of flatus or stool, tolerated oral diet and nasogastric tube removed.
Renal function and serum potassium normalised.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Outpatient General Surgery follow-up and explicit safety-netting for recurrent pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling.
